Medication- and Illness-Induced Psychiatric Disorders

medication-induced psychosis · glucocorticoids · Cushing syndrome · delirium versus psychosis · medical workup before a primary diagnosisDid a drug or a disease start this, and is attention intact?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Rule out a drug or a medical illness before diagnosing a primary psychiatric disorder
  • New psychosis on high-dose glucocorticoids, alert and oriented medication-induced psychotic disorder
  • Fluctuating attention and disorientation delirium, with any psychosis secondary
What it is

Psychiatric symptoms caused directly by a drug or a disease, not a primary disorder

Driver

A new medication or dose a disease known to cause psychosis or mood change

Triggers

High-dose glucocorticoids, typically in the first week but at any time

Cushing syndrome, thyroid disease, lupus, Wilson disease, stroke, autoimmune encephalitis

Chain

Drug or disease starts symptoms follow it in time they ease when the cause is treated

Insights

Timing decides: what started before the symptoms, a drug, a dose or a disease?

Cushing syndrome can be mistaken for a primary depressive or anxiety disorder

Medical causes by systemdetail behind the triggers
EndocrineCushing syndrome (low or labile mood, anxiety, insomnia); hypothyroidism with depression; hyperthyroidism with anxiety; hypercalcemia with depression
AutoimmuneLupus: psychosis with arthralgia, low platelets and hematuria in a young womananti-N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor encephalitis: psychiatric change, memory loss, seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability; ovarian teratoma
NeurologicStroke or a tumor, seizures, Wilson disease
OtherMetabolic or electrolyte disorders, central nervous system infection
3Differential
Drug, disease or primary disorder, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Medication-induced psychotic disorder (substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder)Acute delusions or hallucinations after a new medication; alert, orientedBegins with the new drug; steroids: typically in the first week
Fluctuating attention and disorientation; psychosis secondaryHours to days, fluctuating; attention fails
Psychotic disorder due to another medical conditionHistory, examination or labs show a disease known to cause psychosisBegins and ends with the illness
Onset before 40, a prodrome, auditory hallucinations, family historyNo drug or disease explains it; then time it
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Paranoid and disoriented to time after surgery, on meperidineDelirium from a highly deliriogenic opioidFind and treat the cause
Onset after 40 with a speech or motor deficitA structural cause such as strokeImage the brain before an antipsychotic
Depression with cold intolerance and lethargyHypothyroidismThyroid tests
Multiple sclerosis: relapsing neurologic episodes, white matter lesionsNot conversion or dementiaThe symptoms are due to a known neurologic disease, and patients with multiple sclerosis are not at increased risk of conversion or somatic symptom disorder. Anxiety about the illness is common, but it does not point to generalized anxiety disorder or panic disorder. Cognitive impairment is common, frank dementia is not, and untreated depression worsens it.Psychotherapy and an antidepressant; psychosis may come from high-dose steroids, rarely the disease itself
Parkinson disease with controlled movement, new anhedonia, and altered sleep or appetiteDepression associated with Parkinson disease Distinguishing featuresMasked facial expression and slow movement overlap depression. Sadness and loss of pleasure with social withdrawal favor depression over apathy. Daytime sleepiness with anhedonia does not by itself justify reducing effective levodopa.Treat with an antidepressant and/or psychotherapy; maintain effective motor therapy.
Panic attacks with stable thyroid disease (normal thyroid-stimulating hormone, TSH) and rare albuterol usePanic disorder, not anxiety from the condition or the drugKeep panic disorder as the diagnosis; name a medical or drug cause only when it directly causes the attacks (eg, too much levothyroxine or albuterol)
New depression or panic with Cushing featuresCushing syndromeExclude exogenous glucocorticoids, then test for hypercortisolism before an antidepressant
New depression and anxiety in an older smoker with marked weight loss and new diabetes without obesityPancreatic cancer ImagingIn a nonjaundiced patient with weight loss, CT of the abdomen is the preferred first test; ultrasound is for the jaundiced patient.CT scan of the abdomen before an antidepressant
Pause point
New symptoms in a patient with a medication or a medical disease Offered: starting risperidone or an antidepressant The drug, dose or disease began first → Find the cause before naming a primary disorder

Once a known disease explains the depression (eg, multiple sclerosis), treat the depression too.

5Diagnostic criteria
Defining features
LabelFeature
Medication-inducedAcute delusions or hallucinations temporally linked to a new medication
Due to another medical conditionA disease known to cause psychosis (eg, central nervous system tumor, stroke, endocrine or autoimmune disorder), beginning and ending with it
DeliriumFluctuating cognition with poor attention and disorientation
Favors a primary psychosisOnset before 40, a prodrome, auditory (not visual, gustatory or tactile) hallucinations, family history of psychotic illness
7Treatment
1

Firstsevere glucocorticoid psychosis or mania

Lower the prednisone dose to under 40 mg/day, or as low as the illness allows

Avoid an aggressive taper: withdrawal risk.

2

Thenthe dose cannot be reduced

A low-dose antipsychotic

Case reports only; lithium has been described for prevention, with more side effects.

By cause
CauseDo
Due to a medical conditionTreat the condition; some patients also need treatment for the psychosis itself
Cushing features with depression or anxietyTest for hypercortisolism before starting an antidepressant; exclude exogenous glucocorticoids first, the most common cause
Delirium
8Follow-up
Follow-up decisions
WhenDo
No drug or disease foundDiagnose the primary disorder: time the psychosis, or apply the depression criteria
Cause treatedPsychosis often eases; some patients still need treatment for the psychosis itself
Practice
  1. 64-year-old woman, day 10 of prednisone 60 mg daily for giant cell arteritis for 2 days sure neighbors poison her water; hears them plotting no psychiatric history or drug use alert, attentive, oriented · T 36.9 °C · examination otherwise normal → Medication-induced psychotic disorder → new delusions and hallucinations during high-dose prednisone (typical in the first week but possible at any time), with attention and orientation intact; delirium centers on fluctuating attention and disorientation, and brief psychotic disorder is excluded when a medication better explains the symptoms
  2. 57-year-old woman, 3 weeks of believing neighbors spy on her first psychiatric symptoms ever; no family history new trouble finding words; right hand clumsy alert and oriented · BP 138/84 mm Hg · toxicology, chemistry and thyroid tests normal → Brain MRI → onset after 40 with a speech and motor deficit points to a structural cause such as a stroke: image the brain before starting risperidone for a presumed primary psychosis; electroencephalography is for suspected seizure activity
  3. 78-year-old man on high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone for a lung flare since yesterday picks at the air, calls the nurse by his wife's name clear at noon, muddled by evening cannot name months backward · oriented to person only · T 37.2 °C → Delirium → fluctuating attention with disorientation is the core of delirium, and psychotic features may appear secondarily; here attention and orientation fail, whereas an alert, oriented patient makes delirium less likely; brief psychotic disorder is excluded when a medication or medical illness better explains the symptoms
  4. 36-year-old man, 3 months of panic attacks and poor sleep facial flushing; bruises easily; trouble rising from a chair uses no steroid pills, inhalers or creams BP 150/96 mm Hg · wide purple striae on the flanks · fasting glucose 128 mg/dL → 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test → panic attacks and insomnia with facial flushing, easy bruising, wide violaceous striae, proximal weakness, hypertension and high glucose suggest Cushing syndrome once exogenous glucocorticoids are excluded; rule out the medical cause before treating with sertraline, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor). Insulin-like growth factor 1 screens for acromegaly, which enlarges the jaw, hands and feet. The first test is chosen by suitability: late-night salivary cortisol may not suit variable bedtimes, and a 24-hour urinary free cortisol is also accepted
  5. 52-year-old man, day 6 of prednisone 60 mg daily for colitis no sleep for 3 nights; spent his savings says he can cure cancer; no psychiatric history; bowels improving alert and oriented · neurologic examination normal · HR 88/min · T 36.8 °C → Taper the prednisone dose → severe glucocorticoid-induced mania: dose reduction comes first, toward under 40 mg/day of prednisone or the lowest dose possible while the colitis allows; lithium has been described for prevention and has more side effects, and imaging is for a focal or cognitive finding
  6. 19-year-old man, 2 months of paranoia and irritability; grades falling slurred speech and an unsteady gait no drug use; urine toxicology negative T 36.7 °C · alanine aminotransferase 112 U/L · thyroid tests normal → Serum ceruloplasmin → psychosis with dysarthria, ataxia and abnormal liver tests points to Wilson disease: serum ceruloplasmin, with 24-hour urinary copper, before starting risperidone; a heavy metal screen is for cognitive deficits, ataxia, choreoathetosis and polyneuropathy, and dysarthria with abnormal liver tests is the Wilson pattern
Pairs with Psychosis: no drug or medical cause, then time it. Delirium: is attention fluctuating? Major Depressive Disorder: criteria met with no medical cause. Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism: motor disease, mimics and disease complications.
Transferable rule

Before naming a psychiatric disorder, ask what started before the symptoms: a drug, a dose, or a disease.
